1.problem: Ducks either live in Duckland or Sadland, and ducks either can quack or cannot. It is known that \(\frac{9}{10}\) of the ducks in Duckland can quack, and \(\frac{9}{10}\) of the ducks who can quack live in Duckland. Moreover, \(\frac{14}{15}\) of the ducks who cannot quack live in Sadland. The fraction of all ducks who can quack can be expressed as \(\frac{m}{n}\), where \(m\) and \(n\) are relatively prime positive integers. Find \(m + n\).
1.solutions: Let there be \(x\) ducks who live in Duckland but cannot quack. Since \(\frac{9}{10}\) of the ducks in Duckland can quack, there are \(9x\) ducks in Duckland who can quack. Since \(\frac{9}{10}\) of the ducks who quack live in Duckland, \(9x\) must also be \(9\) times the number of ducks who can quack but don’t live in Duckland, thus there are \(x\) ducks that can quack but don’t live in Duckland. Therefore there are \(10x\) total ducks that can quack. Since there are \(x\) ducks who cannot quack but live in Duckland, and these make up \(1 - \frac{14}{15} = \frac{1}{15}\) of the ducks that cannot quack, there are \(15x\) total ducks that cannot quack and \(25x\) total ducks. Thus \(\frac{a}{b} = \frac{10x}{25x} = \frac{2}{5}\), so we get an answer of \(7\).

2.problem: If \(x\) and \(y\) are real numbers satisfying \(y = \frac{1000}{1001}x - 10\) and \(y = -\frac{1001}{1000}x + 10\), find the value of \(x^2 + y^2\).
2.solutions: Notice the lines \(y = \frac{1000}{1001}x - 10\) and \(y = -\frac{1001}{1000}x + 10\) have slopes multiplying to \(-1\), and hence are perpendicular. Then let \(A = (0, 10)\), \(B = (0, -10)\), and \(C = (a, b)\) be the point of intersection of the two lines. Then \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) form a right triangle with hypotenuse \(AB\). Further, the circumcenter of a right triangle is the midpoint of its hypotenuse, which here is \(O = (0, 0)\). Then \(a^2 + b^2 = OC^2\) just by the distance formula! And as \(O\) is the circumcenter of \(\triangle ABC\), we hence want to compute \(R^2\) where \(R\) is the circumradius of \(\triangle ABC\). Then as \(\triangle ABC\) is right, its circumradius is half the length of its hypotenuse, which has length \(AB = 20\). Then \(R = 10\) and hence \(a^2 + b^2 = 10^2 = 100\).

3.problem: Jacqueline marks a nonzero number of vertices of a unit cube. In how many ways can Jacqueline accomplish this so that all marked vertices lie on some plane? If two markings of the cube are the same when rotated, they are still counted as distinct.
3.solutions:
Jacqueline always succeeds if she marks at most three points: this contributes \(\binom{8}{1} + \binom{8}{2} + \binom{8}{3} = 92\) possibilities. If she marks four points, there are two possibilities:

  • All four points lie on the same face: \(+6\).
  • Two points form the diagonal of one face, and the other two points form the diagonal of the opposite face: \(+6\).

It is impossible for Jacqueline to draw more than four points. So there are \(92 + 6 + 6 = 104\) ways in total.

4.problem: A three-reel slot machine shows a 3-digit display string \(N\) (digits may include a leading zero). When the lever is pulled, the reels rotate so that the last digit moves to the front. That is, if \(N\) is \(abc\), the new display will be \(cab\). Strangely, the machine pays a jackpot whenever the new display is exactly 198 larger than the original (when read as 3-digit numbers). Find the number of 3-digit display strings \(N\) that trigger a jackpot.
4.solutions: Let the display be \[N = 100a + 10b + c,\] where \(a, b, c \in \{0, \ldots, 9\}\) (leading zero allowed). After the shift, the display becomes \[100c + 10a + b.\] The jackpot condition says: \[100c + 10a + b = (100a + 10b + c) + 198.\] Rearranging, \[\begin{aligned} 100c + 10a + b - 100a - 10b - c &= 198\\ \Rightarrow 99c - 90a - 9b &= 198\\ \Rightarrow 11c - 10a - b &= 22. \quad (\star) \end{aligned}\] Working modulo 11, we have \[11c - 10a - b \equiv 0 \pmod{11}.\] Since \(11c \equiv 0 \pmod{11}\) and \(-10 \equiv 1 \pmod{11}\), we get: \[-10a - b \equiv 0 \pmod{11} \Rightarrow a - b \equiv 0 \pmod{11}.\] Thus, \[b = a,\] since \(a, b \in \{0, \ldots, 9\}\). Plugging \(b = a\) into \((\star)\), we have \[11c - 10a - a = 22 \Rightarrow 11c - 11a = 22 \Rightarrow c - a = 2 \Rightarrow c = a + 2.\] To ensure \(c \le 9\), we require \(a \le 7\). Since leading zeros are now allowed, \(a\) may be \(0\). Then the number is: \[N = 100a + 10b + (a+2) = 111a + 2,\] for \(a = 0, 1, \ldots, 7\). The valid strings are \[002, 113, 224, 335, 446, 557, 668, 779,\] giving an answer of \(8\).

5.problem: For some real number \(a\), the polynomial \[20x^4 - 161x^3 + ax^2 - 161x + 20\] has four distinct real roots, whose median is \(\frac{41}{40}\). What is \(a\)?
5.solutions:
Solution 1. Let \(P(x) = 20x^4 - 161x^3 + ax^2 - 161x + 20\). Since clearly \(x = 0\) is not a solution to \(P(x) = 0\), divide both sides by \(x^2\). We get \(20x^2 - 161x + a - \frac{161}{x} + \frac{20}{x^2} = 0\), factoring and using the identity \((x + \frac1x)^2 = x^2 + \frac{1}{x^2} + 2\) we get \(20(x + \frac1x)^2 - 161(x + \frac1x) + a - 40 = 0\) if and only if \(P(x) = 0\). If we substitute \(x\) with \(\frac1x\), the polynomial doesn’t change, so if \(r\) is a root, \(\frac1r\) is also a root. Hence, our roots are in two groups of reciprocals. If both are negative then the median is negative so that does not work. If one is negative and the other is positive, then the two terms that contribute to the median will be in the intervals \((-1, 0)\) and \((0, 1)\) so the median will be in \((-1, 1)\), so this does not work. Therefore all four roots are positive. Let these roots be \(0 < r_1 < r_2 < 1 < r_3 < r_4\), so \(r_2 + r_3 = r_2 + \frac{1}{r_2} = \frac{41}{20}\). Now notice that \(r_2 + r_3\) and \(r_1 + r_4\) correspond to the solutions \(y\) of \(20y^2 - 161y + a - 40 = 0\), so Vieta gives \(r_1 + r_4 = 6\) and thus \(a - 40 = 6 \cdot 41\) and thus our final answer is \(a = 286\).

Solution 2. Using the same work with signs as above, we get \(0 < r_1 < r_2 < r_3 < r_4\) and \(r_1 r_4 = r_2 r_3 = 1\). Vieta gives \(\frac{161}{120} = r_1 + r_2 + r_3 + r_4\) and median gives \(r_2 + r_3 = \frac{41}{20}\) so \(r_1 + r_4 = 6\). Then Vieta with \(a\) gives us \(\frac{a}{20} = r_1 r_2 + r_1 r_3 + r_1 r_4 + r_2 r_3 + r_2 r_4 + r_3 r_4 = (r_1 + r_4)(r_2 + r_3) + r_1 r_4 + r_2 r_3 = 6 \cdot \frac{41}{20} + 2 = \frac{286}{20}\) so we once again get \(286\).

Solution 3. Using \(P(x)\) and values of \(r\) as shown above, this can be solved using substitution. We have \(r_2 r_3 = 1\) and \(r_2 + r_3 = \frac{41}{20}\) so using Vieta to construct a quadratic we can solve and get \(r_2 = \frac45\) and \(r_3 = \frac54\). Since both of these are roots, just pick one and plug it into \(P\). We know \(P(r_2) = P(\frac45) = 0\) and substituting into our definition of \(P\) we can compute \(a = 286\).

6.problem: Let \(ABC\) be a triangle with \(AB = 25\) and \(AC = 15\). The bisector of \(\angle A\) meets \(\overline{BC}\) at a point \(D\). The altitudes from \(B\) and \(C\) meet \(\overline{AC}\) and \(\overline{AB}\) respectively at points \(E\) and \(F\). If \(\overline{EF}\) passes through the midpoint of \(\overline{AD}\), what is \(BC^2\)?
6.solutions: Let \(C'\) be the reflection of \(C\) across \(\overline{AD}\) and let \(B'\) be the reflection of \(B\) across \(\overline{AD}\). By orthic triangle angle properties, \(\triangle AEF \sim \triangle AB'C'\) and since \(D\) lies on \(\overline{B'C'}\), \(\overline{EF}\) is the result of taking homothety of size \(\frac12\) centered at \(A\) on \(\overline{B'C'}\). Hence \(AE = \frac{AC'}{2} = \frac{AC}{2} = \frac{25}{2}\) and thus \(\triangle AEB\) is a \(30\)-\(60\)-\(90\) triangle and we get \(\angle A = 60^\circ\) and thus the Law of Cosines gives us our final answer of \(BC^2 = AB^2 + AC^2 - AB \cdot BC = 625 + 225 - 375 = 475\).

7.problem: How many permutations of the integers \(\{1, 2, \ldots, 67\}\) satisfy the property that for any \(7\) consecutive elements, their sum is divisible by \(7\), and for any \(9\) consecutive elements, their sum is divisible by \(9\)?
7.solutions: First, let \(a_i\) denote the \(i\)th element in the permutation. Since \[a_i + a_{i+1} + a_{i+2} + a_{i+3} + a_{i+4} + a_{i+5} + a_{i+6} \equiv a_{i+1} + a_{i+2} + a_{i+3} + a_{i+4} + a_{i+5} + a_{i+6} + a_{i+7} \equiv 0 \pmod 7\] we must have that \(a_i \equiv a_{i+7} \pmod 7\). We can similarly obtain that \(a_i \equiv a_{i+9} \pmod 9\). Combining these with Chinese Remainder Theorem (7 and 9 are coprime) we get that \(a_{i+63} \equiv a_i \pmod{63}\). The only duplicates mod 63 are 1 with 64, 2 with 65, 3 with 66, and 4 with 67. This means that these eight elements must be the first four and last four elements in our sequence, giving us that the first 63 elements must contain every possible residue mod 63. However, we know that the numbers cycle every 7 terms mod 7, and every 9 terms mod 9, and due to the equal distributions, we get that each cycle contains each possible residue once, and thus CRT will determine our first 63 terms (up to mod 63) once these permutations are chosen. We have \(4!\) ways to arrange our first four terms mod 63, and then \(3!\) ways to choose our remaining order mod 7, and \(5!\) for 9. We then have \(2^4\) ways to swap our terms that are equivalent mod 63, so our final answer is \[3! \cdot 4! \cdot 5! \cdot 2^4 = 6 \cdot 24 \cdot 120 \cdot 16 = 276480\]

8.problem: Daniel has one bomb-duck. On the 17th of each month, each bomb-duck either self-destructs with probability \(\frac12\), or gives birth to \(n\) bomb-ducks with probability \(\frac{1}{2^{n+1}}\) (for example, there is a \(\frac14\) chance of giving birth to 1 bomb-duck, a \(\frac18\) chance of giving birth to 2 bomb-ducks, and so on). The probability that Daniel eventually has no bomb-ducks can be expressed as \(\frac{m}{n}\), where \(m\) and \(n\) are relatively prime positive integers. Find \(m + n\).
8.solutions: Define \(P(n)\) to be the probability of eventually having no bomb-ducks if you start with \(n\) bomb-ducks. We are trying to find \(P(1)\). First, we claim that for all positive integers \(n\), \(P(n) = P(1)^n\). Imagine you start with \(n\) bomb-ducks, and create \(n\) rooms, each with one bomb-duck. These rooms never interact, the same way Bomb-ducks are independent of the offspring of other Bomb-ducks. Hence \(P(n)\) is the probability that all the rooms end up empty, and the probability of any given room ending up empty is \(P(1)\), so \(P(n) = P(1)^n\). Now we will use the probability distribution, assuming that bomb-ducks themselves do not die from giving birth. We have \[P(1) = \frac12 + \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \frac{P(n)}{2^n} = \frac12 + \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \left( \frac{P(1)}{2} \right)^n = \frac12 + \frac{P(1)^2}{4} \left( \frac{1}{1 - \frac{P(1)}{2}} \right)\] by using the formula for an infinite geometric series. We can then solve this quadratic to get either \(P(1) = \frac23\) or \(P(1) = 1\). Since we start with a \(\frac12\) chance of extinction, the probability will approach \(\frac23\) rather than \(1\), so our final answer is \(2 + 3 = 5\).

9.problem: How many ordered pairs of integers \((x, y)\) with \(0 \le x, y \le 2026\) satisfy \(y^2 \equiv x^3 + 2 \pmod{2027}\)?
9.solutions: For any prime \(p \equiv 2 \pmod 3\), we claim that the map \(x \mapsto x^3\) on is bijective mod \(p\). Let \(g\) be such that \(\{1, g, g^2, \cdots, g^{p-2}\}\) are all distinct. Then every element in \(\{1, 2, \cdots, p-1\}\) can be written as \(g^k\) for some \(k \in \{0, 1, \ldots, p-2\}\). The map \(x \mapsto x^3\) sends \[g^k \mapsto (g^k)^3 = g^{3k}.\] Thus it corresponds to the map \(k \mapsto 3k \pmod{p-1}\), which is a bijection since \(p - 1 \equiv 1 \pmod 3\). It follows that \(x^3 + 2\) attains every value mod 2027 exactly once as \(x\) ranges from \(0\) to \(2026\). So for every \(y\), there is exactly one \(x\) such that \(y^2 = x^3 + 2\). It follows that there are \(2027\) such ordered pairs.

10.problem: Let \(\zeta = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{2025}}\). The value of \[\sum_{i=0}^{2024} \left( \sum_{j=0}^{1012} \zeta^{ij} \right)^{-1}\] can be expressed as \(a + \frac1b\) for positive integers \(a\) and \(b\) with \(b\) greater than \(1\). Find \(a + b\).
10.solutions: We first isolate \(i = 0\). We get \[\sum_{i=0}^{2024} \left( \sum_{j=0}^{1012} \zeta^{ij} \right)^{-1} = \sum_{i=1}^{2024} \left( \sum_{j=0}^{1012} \zeta^{ij} \right)^{-1} + \left( \sum_{j=0}^{1012} \zeta^{0j} \right)^{-1} = \sum_{i=1}^{2024} \left( \sum_{j=0}^{1012} \zeta^{ij} \right)^{-1} + \frac{1}{1013}\] Now, we want to evaluate \(\sum_{i=1}^{2024} \left( \sum_{j=0}^{1012} \zeta^{ij} \right)^{-1}\). First, use the infinite series formula on the inner sum to get \[\left( \sum_{j=0}^{1012} z^{ij} \right)^{-1} = \left( \frac{z^{1013i} - 1}{z^i - 1} \right)^{-1} = \frac{z^i - 1}{z^{1013i} - 1}\] Now we will use the roots of unity formula (\(z\) is just a primitive 2025th root of unity) to get that \(z^{2025i} = 1\) and get the following (crux step): \[\frac{z^i - 1}{z^{1013i} - 1} = \frac{z^{2026i} - 1}{z^{1013i} - 1} = z^{1013i} + 1\] by difference of squares. From here: \[\sum_{i=1}^{2024} \left( \sum_{j=0}^{1012} z^{ij} \right)^{-1} = \sum_{i=1}^{2024} z^{1013i} + 1 = 2024 + \sum_{i=1}^{2024} z^{1013i} = 2024 - 1 = 2023\] (since 1013 and 2025 are coprime, we are adding all roots of unity besides 1 so the sum will be \(-1\)) and hence our expression is \(2023 + \frac{1}{1013}\) and our answer is \(2023 + 1013 = 3036\).

11.problem: Let \(ABCD\) be a tetrahedron with \(AB = 7\), \(AC = AD = 6\), \(BC = BD = 5\), and \(CD = 4\), and let \(G\) be its centroid. Let \(A_1\), \(B_1\), \(C_1\), and \(D_1\) be the circumcenters of tetrahedra \(BCDG\), \(ACDG\), \(ABDG\), and \(ABCG\), respectively, and let \(G_1\) be the centroid of tetrahedron \(A_1B_1C_1D_1\). The ratio of the volume of polyhedron \(A_1BCDG_1\) to the volume of \(A_1B_1C_1D_1\) can be expressed as \(\frac{m}{n}\), where \(m\) and \(n\) are relatively prime positive integers. Find \(m + n\).
11.solutions:
Let \(\vec{A} = \mathbf{a}\), \(\vec{B} = \mathbf{b}\), \(\vec{C} = \mathbf{c}\), and \(\vec{D} = \mathbf{d}\). Let \(\vec{A_1} = \mathbf{u}\), \(\vec{B_1} = \mathbf{v}\), \(\vec{C_1} = \mathbf{w}\), and \(\vec{D_1} = \mathbf{x}\). First we show that \(G_1\) is the center of the sphere through \(A\), \(B\), \(C\), and \(D\).

WLOG, let \(G\) lie on the origin. Then \(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{d} = \vec{0}\). Since \(A_1\) is equidistant from \(B\), \(C\), \(D\), and \(G\), \[\|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{b}\| = \|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{c}\| = \|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{d}\| = \|\mathbf{u}\|,\] \[(\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{b}) \cdot (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{b}) = (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{c}) \cdot (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{c}) = (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{d}) \cdot (\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{d}) = \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{u}.\] Similarly, \[(\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{a}) = (\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{c}) \cdot (\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{c}) = (\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{d}) \cdot (\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{d}) = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}\] \[(\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{a}) = (\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{b}) \cdot (\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{b}) = (\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{d}) \cdot (\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{d}) = \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{w}\] \[(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) = (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}) = (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}) = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{x}\] It suffices to show that \[\|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w} + \mathbf{x} - 4\mathbf{a}\| = \|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w} + \mathbf{x} - 4\mathbf{b}\|\] \[= \|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w} + \mathbf{x} - 4\mathbf{c}\| = \|\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w} + \mathbf{x} - 4\mathbf{d}\|\] or \[2\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} - \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w} + \mathbf{x}) = 2\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{b} \cdot (\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w} + \mathbf{x})\] \[= 2\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{c} \cdot (\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w} + \mathbf{x}) = 2\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{d} - \mathbf{d} \cdot (\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w} + \mathbf{x}).\] Note that \((\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{a}) = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}\) implies \(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 2(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{v})\). By symmetry, \[2\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} - \mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w} + \mathbf{x}) = \frac12 \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} + (\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{d}) \cdot \mathbf{u} = \frac12(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{d}),\] which completes the proof.

Thus \(A_1G_1 \perp BCD\), \(B_1G_1 \perp ACD\), \(C_1G_1 \perp ABD\), and \(D_1G_1 \perp ABC\).

Now we show that \[\frac{A_1G_1}{[\triangle BCD]} = \frac{B_1G_1}{[\triangle ACD]} = \frac{C_1G_1}{[\triangle ABD]} = \frac{D_1G_1}{[\triangle ABC]}.\] Note that \[\overrightarrow{A_1G_1} = e(\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c}) \times (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{d}) = 2e[\triangle BCD]\vec{n}_{BCD}\] \[\overrightarrow{B_1G_1} = f(\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{a}) \times (\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{d}) = 2f[\triangle ACD]\vec{n}_{CAD}\] \[\overrightarrow{C_1G_1} = g(\mathbf{d} - \mathbf{a}) \times (\mathbf{d} - \mathbf{b}) = 2g[\triangle ABD]\vec{n}_{DAB}\] \[\overrightarrow{D_1G_1} = h(\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{c}) \times (\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b}) = 2h[\triangle ABC]\vec{n}_{ACB},\] for some scalars \(e\), \(f\), \(g\), and \(h\). Since \(G_1\) is the centroid of \(A_1B_1C_1D_1\), \[\vec{0} = \overrightarrow{A_1G_1} + \overrightarrow{B_1G_1} + \overrightarrow{C_1G_1} + \overrightarrow{D_1G_1}\] \[= (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{c}) \times (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{d}) + (\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{a}) \times (\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{d}) + (\mathbf{d} - \mathbf{a}) \times (\mathbf{d} - \mathbf{b}) + (\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{c}) \times (\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b})\] \[= (f - e)(\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{a}) \times (\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{d}) + (g - e)(\mathbf{d} - \mathbf{a}) \times (\mathbf{d} - \mathbf{b}) + (h - e)(\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{c}) \times (\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{b}).\] Since the normal vectors of any three faces of \(ABCD\) are linearly independent, \(e = f = g = h\), as desired. Thus \[\frac{\text{Vol}(A_1BCDG_1)}{[\triangle BCD]^2} = \frac{\text{Vol}(AB_1CDG_1)}{[\triangle ACD]^2} = \frac{\text{Vol}(ABC_1DG_1)}{[\triangle ABD]^2} = \frac{\text{Vol}(ABCD_1G_1)}{[\triangle ABC]^2}.\] Since \(A\) and \(G\) are equidistant from each of \(B_1\), \(C_1\), and \(D_1\), \(\triangle B_1C_1D_1\) lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(\overline{AG}\) and \(\text{Vol}(AB_1C_1D_1) = \text{Vol}(GB_1C_1D_1)\). Thus by symmetry, \[\text{Vol}(A_1B_1C_1D_1)\] \[= \frac12\left(\text{Vol}(AB_1C_1D_1G) + \text{Vol}(A_1BC_1D_1G) + \text{Vol}(A_1B_1CD_1G) + \text{Vol}(A_1B_1C_1DG)\right)\] \[= \frac12\left(\text{Vol}(A_1BCDG_1) + \text{Vol}(AB_1CDG_1) + \text{Vol}(ABC_1DG_1) + \text{Vol}(ABCD_1G_1)\right)\] Thus \[\frac{\text{Vol}(A_1BCDG_1)}{\text{Vol}(A_1B_1C_1D_1)} = \frac{2[\triangle BCD]^2}{[\triangle BCD]^2 + [\triangle ACD]^2 + [\triangle ABD]^2 + [\triangle ABC]^2}\] \[= \frac{2 \cdot 84}{84 + 128 + 216 + 216} = \frac{6}{23},\] giving an answer of \(29\).

12.problem: A collection of dots is arranged in the shape of an equilateral triangle with 2025 dots on each side. What is the maximum number of dots that can be chosen from the arrangement such that no two chosen dots lie on a line parallel to any side? An example arrangement with 4 dots on each side is shown below.
12.solutions:
We show that the maximum number of dots that can be chosen is \(\left\lfloor \frac{2n+1}{3} \right\rfloor\). Note that every dot in the configuration can be represented by an ordered triple of nonnegative integers \((a, b, c)\), where the \(i\)th coordinate represents the distance from that point to the \(i\)th side along the direction of either of the other two sides. We note

  1. The coordinates of every dot satisfy \(a + b + c = n - 1\).
  2. Two dots lie on a line parallel to the same side if and only if they share one coordinate.

Now suppose \(m\) dots can chosen in such a way that no two chosen dots lie on a line parallel to any side. The sum of all \(3m\) coordinates is \(m(n-1)\). Since all \(i\)th coordinates are distinct, the sum of all \(i\)th coordinates must be greater than or equal to \[0 + 1 + \ldots + (m-1) = \frac{m(m-1)}{2}\] for each \(i\). Thus we have \[\begin{aligned} m(n-1) &\ge \frac{3m(m-1)}{2}\\ n - 1 &\ge \frac{3(m-1)}{2}\\ \frac{2n+1}{3} &\ge m, \end{aligned}\] which is the desired bound. When \(n = 2025\), we can choose at most \(\left\lfloor \frac{2 \cdot 2025 + 1}{3} \right\rfloor = 1350\) dots, and a construction is given by the coordinates below. \[(675, 1349, 0), (674, 1348, 2), (673, 1347, 4), \ldots, (0, 674, 1350)\] \[(1350, 673, 1), (1349, 672, 3), (1348, 671, 5), \ldots, (677, 0, 1347)\]
